passage:
Every September, a little before dark, the chimney swifts of Wenbury gather over the old Linden Row School. The first evening I watched them, I took the circling flock for smoke from the school's furnace, which has been cold for eleven years. As the sun drops behind Calder Ridge, the bank of windows along the school's west wall goes dark, and the first swifts drop into the chimney. By the time the church clock strikes seven, every bird is inside, well before the last children leave the schoolyard, the last bus passes the school gates and the streetlights on the hill come on.

Tomas Reyburn was caretaker at Linden Row for thirty years, and he lit that furnace every winter morning until the day the school closed. Since 1996 he has stood in the schoolyard each September evening with a hand counter, and his first notebooks record a roost of nine and ten thousand birds. This year's best was 640. He keeps the old notebooks in a drawer now, and says the one in his pocket will last him the rest of his life.

In the storm two winters ago, a crack opened near the top of the chimney, and before morning the top third had fallen into the schoolyard. Reyburn knew the council would vote to keep the stump standing and cap it rather than have it pulled down, since capping cost less, and it did. The masons relaid the top courses of brick in lime mortar rather than cheap cement and set a smooth stone cap over them, leaving the flue open. The stump is sound.

The chimney I know is only the stump of the one Reyburn knew, and the evenings when ten thousand swifts poured into it are gone for good. The shortened flue holds a few hundred birds at most.

In early October the birds will leave for the south, and in May they will return to the same stump. Each September evening the few hundred that remain drop into it within a few minutes, and then the sky over Linden Row is empty long before the old flocks would have finished coming down.
